title: The Canvas and the Game Loop
subtitle:
Every version of Asteroids in this collection starts the same way: a
      <canvas> sized to fill its box, and a loop that keeps redrawing it
      at the screen's refresh rate. Nothing moves yet — this lesson is
      just about getting that skeleton running correctly, including on a
      phone, where the canvas has to handle high-DPI screens and window
      resizes without turning blurry.
body:
A canvas that fills its box

The canvas lives inside a wrapper div rather than being sized directly, so its CSS box (rounded corners, a fixed aspect ratio, a max width on large screens) is separate from the canvas's own pixel buffer, which the JavaScript below manages.

HTML + CSS
<div class="canvas-wrap" id="canvasWrap">
  <canvas id="gameCanvas"></canvas>
</div>

<style>
  .canvas-wrap {
    width: 100%;
    max-width: 420px;
    aspect-ratio: 3 / 4;
    position: relative;
    background: var(--board);
    border-radius: 20px;
    overflow: hidden;
    box-shadow: 0 10px 30px rgba(0,0,0,0.35);
  }
  #gameCanvas { display: block; width: 100%; height: 100%; }
</style>

Sizing it for real (high-DPI displays)

A canvas actually has two sizes: the CSS size (how big it appears on screen) and the internal pixel buffer size (how many actual pixels you get to draw into). On a phone with devicePixelRatio of 2 or 3, using the CSS size for both leaves you drawing into a buffer with far fewer pixels than the screen has, and everything comes out blurry. resizeCanvas() measures the wrapper, multiplies by dpr for the actual buffer, and then uses ctx.setTransform so every draw call after this can keep working in plain CSS-pixel coordinates without thinking about DPI again.

JavaScript
function resizeCanvas() {
  var rect = canvasWrap.getBoundingClientRect();
  var dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
  var w = Math.round(rect.width);
  var h = Math.round(rect.height);
  if (w === state.canvasCssW && h === state.canvasCssH && dpr === state.canvasDpr) return;
  state.canvasCssW = w;
  state.canvasCssH = h;
  state.canvasDpr = dpr;
  canvas.width = Math.round(w * dpr);
  canvas.height = Math.round(h * dpr);
  canvas.style.width = w + 'px';
  canvas.style.height = h + 'px';
  ctx.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0);
}

var resizeTimer = null;
function onResize() {
  clearTimeout(resizeTimer);
  resizeTimer = setTimeout(resizeCanvas, 150);
}

The early-return guard skips the (moderately expensive) resize work when nothing actually changed, and onResize debounces rapid-fire resize events — both matter more than they look, since mobile browsers fire resize events liberally while the on-screen keyboard shows/hides or the address bar collapses on scroll.

The game loop

requestAnimationFrame asks the browser to call your function right before the next repaint — but it doesn't promise a fixed interval. A phone under load, a background tab, or a 120Hz vs 60Hz screen all change how much time actually passed between frames. So instead of assuming "16ms per frame," the loop measures the real elapsed time (dt, in seconds) and every later lesson's physics multiplies by dt rather than a fixed constant — that's what makes the game run at the same real-world speed regardless of frame rate.

JavaScript
var MAX_DT = 0.05; // clamp dt so a stall (tab backgrounded, etc.) can't cause a huge jump

var rafId = null;
function frame(ts) {
  rafId = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  if (!state.timing.lastFrameTime) { state.timing.lastFrameTime = ts; return; }
  var dt = Math.min((ts - state.timing.lastFrameTime) / 1000, MAX_DT);
  state.timing.lastFrameTime = ts;
  render();
}

The first call has no previous timestamp to diff against, so it just records one and returns — every frame after that computes a real dt. render() for now just clears the canvas; there's nothing to draw until the next lesson.
demoNote: An empty, resizing canvas, running a real loop underneath. Resize your window (or rotate your phone) and it stays sharp.

title: Drawing the Ship
subtitle: Now that the canvas is alive, let's put something on it — the ship, standing still for now (input arrives next lesson). This is also where state shows up: one plain object holding everything about the game world, read by every draw function. That single-object pattern is what the rest of the game is built on.
body:
State as data

Rather than scattering separate variables for the ship's position, heading, and so on, everything lives in one state object. That pays off later: it's the one thing a restart has to reset, the one thing collision code reads from, and the one thing a test can inspect from the outside — which is exactly what the debug hook below is for.

JavaScript
var SHIP_RADIUS = 12;

var state = {
  ship: {
    heading: -Math.PI / 2, // pointing "up"
    radius: SHIP_RADIUS
  },
  canvasCssW: 0, canvasCssH: 0, canvasDpr: 1,
  timing: { lastFrameTime: 0 }
};
window.__astDebugState = state; // read-only hook used by this tutorial's own tests

Heading is in radians, and -Math.PI / 2 means "up" in canvas coordinates — canvas angles increase clockwise from the positive x-axis, so straight up is a quarter turn counter-clockwise from "facing right."

Drawing a rotated shape

Rather than computing each point of a rotated triangle by hand, the canvas has a transform stack: save() remembers where you were, translate()/rotate() move and spin the coordinate system itself, and restore() puts it back. So the ship's shape is drawn as if it always faces along the positive x-axis (angle 0) — the transform handles making it actually point the right way.

JavaScript
var COLOR_SHIP = '#e2e8f0';

function drawShip() {
  var cx = state.canvasCssW / 2, cy = state.canvasCssH / 2;
  var r = state.ship.radius;
  ctx.save();
  ctx.translate(cx, cy);
  ctx.rotate(state.ship.heading);

  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.moveTo(r, 0);
  ctx.lineTo(-r * 0.7, r * 0.7);
  ctx.lineTo(-r * 0.35, 0);
  ctx.lineTo(-r * 0.7, -r * 0.7);
  ctx.closePath();
  ctx.strokeStyle = COLOR_SHIP;
  ctx.lineWidth = 2;
  ctx.stroke();
  ctx.restore();
}

The four points trace a simple arrowhead: a nose out at (r, 0), two back corners, and a notch pulled in at the tail so it reads as a ship rather than a plain triangle. Note it's drawn at the exact center of the canvas every time, regardless of any x/y the ship might have — lesson 4 explains why that's deliberate.

A little atmosphere

Two small functions add a starfield: generateStars() scatters a handful of dots (scaled to the canvas area, so it looks similar on any screen size) whenever the canvas resizes, and drawBackground() paints them each frame, before the ship.

JavaScript
var COLOR_STAR = 'rgba(148, 163, 184, 0.5)';
var stars = [];

function generateStars() {
  stars = [];
  var count = Math.round((state.canvasCssW * state.canvasCssH) / 4000);
  for (var i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    stars.push({
      x: Math.random() * state.canvasCssW,
      y: Math.random() * state.canvasCssH,
      r: Math.random() * 1.2 + 0.3
    });
  }
}

function drawBackground() {
  ctx.fillStyle = COLOR_STAR;
  for (var i = 0; i < stars.length; i++) {
    var s = stars[i];
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.arc(s.x, s.y, s.r, 0, Math.PI * 2);
    ctx.fill();
  }
}

generateStars() gets called at the end of resizeCanvas() from lesson 1, and render() now calls drawBackground() then drawShip(), in that order, so the ship is always drawn on top.
demoNote: A stationary ship over a starfield. It'll start moving in the next lesson.

title: Turning and Thrust
subtitle:
A ship that just sits there isn't a game. This lesson adds keyboard
      input and real vector physics — turning changes a heading angle,
      thrust accelerates the ship along that heading, and a bit of drag
      keeps it from feeling like frictionless deep space (which, ironically,
      is the physically "correct" version — a little damping just
      makes it feel controllable).
body:
Reading the keyboard

Input gets translated into a small set of booleans on state.input, decoupled from how it arrived. The physics code below only ever reads state.input and never touches a keyboard event directly — which matters a lot once lesson 11 needs touch input to drive the exact same flags.

JavaScript
function isLeftKey(code) { return code === 'ArrowLeft' || code === 'KeyA'; }
function isRightKey(code) { return code === 'ArrowRight' || code === 'KeyD'; }
function isThrustKey(code) { return code === 'Space' || code === 'ArrowUp' || code === 'KeyW'; }

document.addEventListener('keydown', function (e) {
  if (isThrustKey(e.code)) e.preventDefault(); // stop Space from scrolling the page
  if (isLeftKey(e.code)) state.input.left = true;
  else if (isRightKey(e.code)) state.input.right = true;
  else if (isThrustKey(e.code)) state.input.thrust = true;
});

document.addEventListener('keyup', function (e) {
  if (isLeftKey(e.code)) state.input.left = false;
  else if (isRightKey(e.code)) state.input.right = false;
  else if (isThrustKey(e.code)) state.input.thrust = false;
});

Turning

Turning is just adding to heading, scaled by dt rather than a fixed amount per frame — the same frame-rate independence idea from lesson 1's game loop. At a TURN_RATE of 3.2 radians/second, holding a turn key for about two seconds spins the ship all the way around.

JavaScript
var TURN_RATE = 3.2; // radians/sec

function updateShip(dt) {
  var ship = state.ship;
  if (state.input.left) ship.heading -= TURN_RATE * dt;
  if (state.input.right) ship.heading += TURN_RATE * dt;
  // ...thrust and drag continue below
}

Thrust, drag, and a speed cap

Thrusting accelerates the ship's velocity vector along its current heading — cos(heading)/sin(heading) split the acceleration into x and y components. Every frame, a damping factor bleeds off a percentage of speed; it's written as Math.pow(1 - DAMPING_PER_SECOND, dt) rather than a flat multiply so the drag rate stays correct regardless of frame rate — the same reasoning as the turn rate above, just for an exponential decay instead of a linear one. Finally, speed is clamped to MAX_SPEED so thrust has a ceiling.

JavaScript
var THRUST_ACCEL = 220;
var MAX_SPEED = 260;
var DAMPING_PER_SECOND = 0.5;

function updateShip(dt) {
  var ship = state.ship;
  if (state.input.left) ship.heading -= TURN_RATE * dt;
  if (state.input.right) ship.heading += TURN_RATE * dt;
  ship.thrusting = state.input.thrust;
  if (ship.thrusting) {
    ship.vx += Math.cos(ship.heading) * THRUST_ACCEL * dt;
    ship.vy += Math.sin(ship.heading) * THRUST_ACCEL * dt;
  }
  var damp = Math.pow(1 - DAMPING_PER_SECOND, dt);
  ship.vx *= damp;
  ship.vy *= damp;
  var speed = Math.sqrt(ship.vx * ship.vx + ship.vy * ship.vy);
  if (speed > MAX_SPEED) {
    var scale = MAX_SPEED / speed;
    ship.vx *= scale;
    ship.vy *= scale;
  }
  ship.x += ship.vx * dt;
  ship.y += ship.vy * dt;
}

That's the whole physics model: no gravity, no friction against anything except the artificial damping — simple enough to reason about, expressive enough to feel like an actual spaceship.

The engine flame

One small addition to last lesson's drawShip(): when ship.thrusting is true, draw a flickering triangle behind the ship before the hull itself, so it renders underneath.

JavaScript
var COLOR_FLAME = '#f97316';

// inside drawShip(), after ctx.rotate(state.ship.heading):
if (state.ship.thrusting) {
  var flameLen = r * (0.8 + Math.random() * 0.5);
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.moveTo(-r * 0.35, r * 0.4);
  ctx.lineTo(-r * 0.35 - flameLen, 0);
  ctx.lineTo(-r * 0.35, -r * 0.4);
  ctx.closePath();
  ctx.fillStyle = COLOR_FLAME;
  ctx.fill();
}

Randomizing the flame's length by a small amount every frame it's drawn is what makes it read as fire rather than a static shape.
demoNote: Arrow keys (or A/D) turn, Up/W/Space thrusts — keyboard only for now, touch controls are lesson 11.

title: The Camera Trick
subtitle: Every rock, bullet, and eventually alien in this game will live in an unbounded "world" coordinate space — the ship's own x/y just keeps growing as it flies around. But lesson 2's drawShip() always draws the ship pinned to the exact center of the canvas. This lesson is the one function that reconciles those two facts — the trick this whole game is built around.
body:
Two coordinate spaces

Think of it as a camera that always points at the ship. The ship has a real position in the world, but on screen it never moves — instead, everything else gets drawn offset by how far the ship has traveled. That offset is the whole function: worldToScreen() takes a world position and returns where it belongs on screen, given where the ship currently is.

JavaScript
function worldToScreen(wx, wy) {
  return {
    x: wx - state.ship.x + state.canvasCssW / 2,
    y: wy - state.ship.y + state.canvasCssH / 2
  };
}

When the ship is at the world origin, that's just "world position plus half the canvas" — the identity you'd expect. As state.ship.x/y grow while the ship flies around, every other object's screen position shifts by exactly the same amount in the opposite direction, which is what makes it look like the world is drifting past a stationary ship rather than the ship moving through a stationary world. Nothing about drawShip() needs to change at all — it was already hard-coded to draw at the canvas center back in lesson 2.

Proving it with an actual rock

Rather than fake this with a placeholder, this checkpoint uses the real asteroid code the next lesson builds on — createRock() makes a rock with an id, an irregular polygon shape, and a size; drawRock() draws it through worldToScreen(), exactly like every other world object will be drawn from here on.

JavaScript
var ROCK_SIZES = {
  large:  { radius: 46, speedRange: [30, 70],   score: 20,  child: 'medium' },
  medium: { radius: 27, speedRange: [50, 100],  score: 50,  child: 'small' },
  small:  { radius: 15, speedRange: [80, 140],  score: 100, child: null }
};

function makeRockShape() {
  var points = [];
  var n = 10 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 4);
  for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    points.push({ angle: (i / n) * Math.PI * 2, r: 0.75 + Math.random() * 0.5 });
  }
  return points; // an irregular polygon, not a plain circle
}

function createRock(size, x, y, vx, vy) {
  return {
    id: state.nextRockId++,
    x: x, y: y, vx: vx, vy: vy,
    rotation: Math.random() * Math.PI * 2,
    rotationSpeed: (Math.random() - 0.5) * 1.6,
    size: size,
    radius: ROCK_SIZES[size].radius,
    shapePoints: makeRockShape()
  };
}
JavaScript
function drawRock(rock) {
  var p = worldToScreen(rock.x, rock.y); // <- the only line that cares about the camera
  ctx.save();
  ctx.translate(p.x, p.y);
  ctx.rotate(rock.rotation);
  ctx.beginPath();
  for (var i = 0; i < rock.shapePoints.length; i++) {
    var pt = rock.shapePoints[i];
    var rad = rock.radius * pt.r;
    var px = Math.cos(pt.angle) * rad;
    var py = Math.sin(pt.angle) * rad;
    if (i === 0) ctx.moveTo(px, py); else ctx.lineTo(px, py);
  }
  ctx.closePath();
  ctx.fillStyle = COLOR_ROCK_FILL;
  ctx.fill();
  ctx.strokeStyle = COLOR_ROCK_STROKE;
  ctx.lineWidth = 2;
  ctx.stroke();
  ctx.restore();
}

This checkpoint parks exactly one rock, with zero velocity, 220 units to the right of where the ship starts: state.rocks.push(createRock('large', 220, 0, 0, 0)). That single line is scaffolding — the next lesson replaces it with a real spawning system that keeps a whole field of rocks drifting around you. Everything else on this page (worldToScreen, createRock, drawRock, ROCK_SIZES) is exactly what ships in the final game, unchanged.
demoNote: Turn to face the rock and thrust toward it. The rock's world position never changes — watch it drift across the screen anyway as the ship's world position moves underneath it.

title: Rocks in an Endless Field
subtitle: This game doesn't wrap rocks around screen edges the way the original arcade cabinet did — there are no edges, since the world is unbounded and the camera just follows the ship (lesson 4). Instead, rocks spawn in a ring just outside what's visible and get cleaned up once they're far enough behind you that they'd never be seen again. This lesson replaces last lesson's single parked rock with that real system.
body:
Seeding the field

When the game starts, seedRocks() scatters six large rocks at random angles around the ship, each already moving in a random direction. Scattering them between 60% of the visible radius and half the despawn radius keeps the very first moment from either dropping a rock right on top of you or spawning one so far out it's invisible.

JavaScript
function randRange(range) { return range[0] + Math.random() * (range[1] - range[0]); }

function visibleRadius() {
  return Math.sqrt(state.canvasCssW * state.canvasCssW + state.canvasCssH * state.canvasCssH) / 2;
}
function despawnRadius() { return visibleRadius() * 2.5; }

function seedRocks() {
  var minDist = visibleRadius() * 0.6;
  var maxDist = despawnRadius() * 0.5;
  for (var i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
    var angle = Math.random() * Math.PI * 2;
    var dist = minDist + Math.random() * (maxDist - minDist);
    var x = state.ship.x + Math.cos(angle) * dist;
    var y = state.ship.y + Math.sin(angle) * dist;
    var dirAngle = Math.random() * Math.PI * 2;
    var speed = randRange(ROCK_SIZES.large.speedRange) * speedMultiplier();
    state.rocks.push(createRock('large', x, y, Math.cos(dirAngle) * speed, Math.sin(dirAngle) * speed));
  }
}

visibleRadius() is the radius of a circle just big enough to cover the whole canvas from its center — the Pythagorean diagonal, halved. Everything about spawning and despawning is expressed relative to it, so it automatically adapts to whatever size screen it's running on.

Spawning ahead, forever

Every half second (SPAWN_CHECK_INTERVAL), if the rock count is under a target that slowly ramps up over time, one more large rock spawns in a ring just past the edge of what's visible (spawnRingRadius()), aimed roughly — not exactly, there's some randomness in the angle — back toward the ship. That inward aim is what makes new rocks feel like a real threat instead of drifting past uselessly off in some random direction.

JavaScript
var SPAWN_CHECK_INTERVAL = 0.5; // seconds

function spawnRingRadius() { return visibleRadius() + 80; }
function targetRockCount() { return Math.min(6 + Math.floor(state.difficulty.elapsed / 30), 14); }
function speedMultiplier() { return 1 + Math.min(state.difficulty.elapsed / 60, 1) * 0.5; }

function trySpawnRocks(dt) {
  state.spawn.timer -= dt;
  if (state.spawn.timer > 0) return;
  state.spawn.timer = SPAWN_CHECK_INTERVAL;
  if (state.rocks.length >= targetRockCount()) return;

  var angle = Math.random() * Math.PI * 2;
  var dist = spawnRingRadius();
  var x = state.ship.x + Math.cos(angle) * dist;
  var y = state.ship.y + Math.sin(angle) * dist;
  var inward = angle + Math.PI + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 1.0;
  var speed = randRange(ROCK_SIZES.large.speedRange) * speedMultiplier();
  state.rocks.push(createRock('large', x, y, Math.cos(inward) * speed, Math.sin(inward) * speed));
}

targetRockCount() and speedMultiplier() both read state.difficulty.elapsed — total seconds played — so the field slowly gets denser and faster the longer you survive, capping out rather than spiraling out of control forever.

Cleaning up behind you

Without some cleanup, a rock spawned five minutes ago and drifting the opposite direction from the ship would still be sitting in the array, updated every frame, forever. despawnFarRocks() just removes anything that's drifted out past despawnRadius() — far enough that it could never be on screen again regardless of where the ship goes next.

JavaScript
function despawnFarRocks() {
  var dr = despawnRadius();
  for (var i = state.rocks.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    var rk = state.rocks[i];
    var dx = rk.x - state.ship.x, dy = rk.y - state.ship.y;
    if (dx * dx + dy * dy > dr * dr) state.rocks.splice(i, 1);
  }
}

function updateRocks(dt) {
  for (var i = 0; i < state.rocks.length; i++) {
    var rk = state.rocks[i];
    rk.x += rk.vx * dt;
    rk.y += rk.vy * dt;
    rk.rotation += rk.rotationSpeed * dt;
  }
}

The loop counts backward specifically so splice() removing an element mid-loop doesn't skip the next one — a classic array-mutation-during-iteration bug avoided by iterating in reverse. update(dt) now calls updateRocks, trySpawnRocks, and despawnFarRocks every frame, alongside updateShip from lesson 3.
demoNote: Fly around for a while. New rocks keep appearing ahead of you no matter which direction you go, and old ones behind you quietly disappear.

title: Shooting
subtitle: One button, two jobs: tap it and the ship fires; hold it and the ship thrusts instead. Getting that distinction right needs an upgrade to the keyboard handler from lesson 3 — and once there's a way to fire, bullets need their own small physics and lifespan.
body:
A bullet, briefly

fireBullet() spawns one bullet at the tip of the ship (ship.radius out along its heading, so it doesn't appear to come from inside the hull), moving at a fixed speed along that same heading. ttl (time to live) counts down every frame; once it hits zero the bullet is removed, so shots don't travel forever.

JavaScript
var BULLET_RADIUS = 3;
var BULLET_SPEED = 480;
var BULLET_LIFETIME = 0.9; // seconds

function fireBullet() {
  var heading = state.ship.heading;
  state.bullets.push({
    x: state.ship.x + Math.cos(heading) * state.ship.radius,
    y: state.ship.y + Math.sin(heading) * state.ship.radius,
    vx: Math.cos(heading) * BULLET_SPEED,
    vy: Math.sin(heading) * BULLET_SPEED,
    ttl: BULLET_LIFETIME
  });
}

function updateBullets(dt) {
  for (var i = state.bullets.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    var b = state.bullets[i];
    b.x += b.vx * dt;
    b.y += b.vy * dt;
    b.ttl -= dt;
    if (b.ttl <= 0) state.bullets.splice(i, 1);
  }
}

(Lesson 9 adds a state.phase !== 'playing' guard at the top of fireBullet(), once there's a game-over state worth respecting — not needed yet.)

Tap to fire, hold to thrust

Lesson 3's thrust key handler engaged thrust the instant the key went down. That's wrong once the same key needs to fire on a quick tap: pressing and immediately releasing shouldn't feel like it thrusted for a single frame. The fix is a short timer — if the key is still down after HOLD_THRESHOLD_MS, then it counts as a hold and thrust engages; if it comes back up before that, it was a tap, and it fires instead.

JavaScript
var HOLD_THRESHOLD_MS = 190;
var kbHoldTimer = null;
var kbHoldEngaged = false;

document.addEventListener('keydown', function (e) {
  if (isThrustKey(e.code)) e.preventDefault();
  if (e.repeat) return; // ignore the OS's auto-repeat keydown spam
  if (isLeftKey(e.code)) state.input.left = true;
  else if (isRightKey(e.code)) state.input.right = true;
  else if (isThrustKey(e.code)) {
    kbHoldEngaged = false;
    kbHoldTimer = setTimeout(function () {
      kbHoldEngaged = true;
      state.input.thrust = true;
    }, HOLD_THRESHOLD_MS);
  }
});

document.addEventListener('keyup', function (e) {
  if (isLeftKey(e.code)) state.input.left = false;
  else if (isRightKey(e.code)) state.input.right = false;
  else if (isThrustKey(e.code)) {
    clearTimeout(kbHoldTimer);
    if (kbHoldEngaged) {
      state.input.thrust = false;
    } else {
      fireBullet();
    }
    kbHoldEngaged = false;
  }
});

e.repeat matters here too: holding a key down makes the browser fire repeated keydown events while it's held, which would otherwise restart the hold-timer over and over and never let it reach HOLD_THRESHOLD_MS. Bailing out on repeats means the timer is only ever started once, by the real initial press.

Rendering bullets is the simplest draw function in the game — just a small filled circle through worldToScreen(), same as every other world object:

JavaScript
function drawBullet(b) {
  var p = worldToScreen(b.x, b.y);
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.arc(p.x, p.y, BULLET_RADIUS, 0, Math.PI * 2);
  ctx.fillStyle = COLOR_BULLET;
  ctx.fill();
}
demoNote: Tap Space/W/Up quickly to fire; hold it down to thrust instead. Bullets vanish after about a second either way — they don't hurt the rocks yet, that's next lesson.

title: Collisions
subtitle: Every object in this game is a circle for physics purposes, however jagged it looks on screen — a rock's polygon shape is just decoration drawn on top of a plain circular collision radius. That one simplification is what makes collision detection cheap enough to check every pair, every single frame.
body:
Two circles overlap when...

...the distance between their centers is less than the sum of their radii. The usual trick: never call Math.sqrt() to get an actual distance if you don't have to — square both sides of the comparison instead. dx*dx + dy*dy <= rr*rr answers exactly the same question as comparing real distances, without the (comparatively expensive) square root, run for every bullet against every rock, every frame.

JavaScript
function handleCollisions() {
  for (var bi = state.bullets.length - 1; bi >= 0; bi--) {
    var b = state.bullets[bi];
    for (var ri = state.rocks.length - 1; ri >= 0; ri--) {
      var rk = state.rocks[ri];
      var dx = b.x - rk.x, dy = b.y - rk.y;
      var rr = rk.radius + BULLET_RADIUS;
      if (dx * dx + dy * dy <= rr * rr) {
        state.bullets.splice(bi, 1);
        state.rocks.splice(ri, 1); // scaffolding - lesson 8 replaces this with splitRock()
        break;
      }
    }
  }
}

Both loops count backward for the same reason lesson 5's despawn loop did: splice() during forward iteration skips whatever shifts into the position you just removed. The break after a hit stops that bullet from also checking the rest of the rocks it can't have hit anymore, since it was just removed.

For now, a hit just deletes the rock outright — no splitting, no score. That line is scaffolding, same idea as lesson 4's parked rock: the detection logic above it (the loops, the distance check) is exactly what ships in the final game; what happens after a hit is what the next two lessons build out. handleCollisions() runs once per frame from update(), after everything has moved for that frame and before the next frame's input is read.
demoNote: Shoot a rock. It disappears outright for now — no pieces, no points. Both land next lesson.

title: Splitting Rocks and Scoring
subtitle: Real Asteroids rewards precision: a big, slow rock is worth less than the small, fast pieces it breaks into. This lesson replaces last lesson's scaffolding (a hit just deletes the rock) with the real splitting logic, and adds the first piece of on-screen HUD so scoring actually has something to show for it.
body:
A small scoreboard

A status bar above the canvas gets a phase indicator (unused until lesson 9) and one score pill. renderHud() is deliberately tiny right now — it'll grow a line at a time as lessons 9 and 10 add lives and a persisted best score to the same bar.

HTML
<div class="status-bar">
  <div class="status-text">
    <span class="turn-dot playing" id="phaseDot"></span>
    <span id="statusLabel">Playing</span>
  </div>
  <div class="scoreboard">
    <div class="score-pill">Score<b id="scoreVal">0</b></div>
  </div>
</div>
JavaScript
function addScore(n) {
  state.score += n;
  renderHud();
}

function renderHud() {
  scoreValEl.textContent = state.score;
}

Splitting, for real

splitRock() replaces last lesson's placeholder. It removes the rock that got hit, awards its size's point value, and — unless it was already the smallest size (child is null for small) — spawns two children one size down. Their launch angle is based on the parent's own direction of travel (or a random angle if the parent happened to be standing still), spread apart symmetrically, so pieces fly outward from the impact rather than in some unrelated direction.

JavaScript
function splitRock(index) {
  var rock = state.rocks[index];
  state.rocks.splice(index, 1);
  var info = ROCK_SIZES[rock.size];
  addScore(info.score);
  if (!info.child) return; // small rocks just vanish

  var baseAngle = (rock.vx || rock.vy) ? Math.atan2(rock.vy, rock.vx) : Math.random() * Math.PI * 2;
  var childInfo = ROCK_SIZES[info.child];
  for (var k = 0; k < 2; k++) {
    var spread = 0.5 + Math.random() * 0.3;
    var ang = baseAngle + (k === 0 ? spread : -spread);
    var speed = randRange(childInfo.speedRange) * speedMultiplier();
    state.rocks.push(createRock(info.child, rock.x, rock.y, Math.cos(ang) * speed, Math.sin(ang) * speed));
  }
}

Back in handleCollisions(), the scaffolding line from lesson 7 becomes a real call: state.rocks.splice(ri, 1) is now splitRock(ri). Recall ROCK_SIZES from lesson 4: large is worth 20, medium 50, small 100 — smaller, faster, harder-to-hit pieces are worth more, which is exactly why the field gets more chaotic (and more rewarding) the longer a big rock survives being whittled down.
demoNote: Shoot a rock. It splits into two smaller ones flying apart, and the score pill climbs — more for the small pieces than the big one they came from.

title: Lives, Game Over, Restart
subtitle: Rocks have been able to hit the ship since lesson 4, but nothing happened when they did — there was no ship side of collision detection at all. This lesson adds it, along with the three things that make losing (and coming back) actually work: lives, a game-over state, and a restart that puts everything back exactly where it started.
body:
The ship's side of a collision

Same squared-distance technique as lesson 7's bullet-vs-rock check, run once against every rock, but only when the ship isn't currently invulnerable — otherwise a respawn would immediately re-trigger another hit before the player has any chance to react.

JavaScript
// added inside handleCollisions(), after the bullet-vs-rock loop:
if (!isInvulnerable()) {
  for (var i = 0; i < state.rocks.length; i++) {
    var rock = state.rocks[i];
    var sx = state.ship.x - rock.x, sy = state.ship.y - rock.y;
    var sr = state.ship.radius + rock.radius;
    if (sx * sx + sy * sy <= sr * sr) {
      shipHit();
      break;
    }
  }
}

function isInvulnerable() { return performance.now() < state.ship.invulnerableUntil; }

Losing a life, or the game

shipHit() is the fork: still got lives left, respawn with a couple seconds of invulnerability; out of lives, end the game instead. respawnShip() deliberately doesn't reset the ship's world position — only its velocity and heading — so respawning doesn't yank the camera back to the origin.

JavaScript
var RESPAWN_INVULN_MS = 2000;

function shipHit() {
  state.lives--;
  if (state.lives <= 0) {
    state.lives = 0;
    endGame();
  } else {
    respawnShip();
  }
  renderHud();
}

function respawnShip() {
  state.ship.vx = 0;
  state.ship.vy = 0;
  state.ship.heading = -Math.PI / 2;
  state.ship.invulnerableUntil = performance.now() + RESPAWN_INVULN_MS;
}

function endGame() {
  state.phase = 'gameover';
  overlayScoreEl.textContent = state.score;
  overlayEl.classList.add('visible');
}

Two more small pieces tie into state.phase: the game loop only calls update(dt) while state.phase === 'playing' (so a game-over screen doesn't keep simulating rocks behind it), and fireBullet() now bails out immediately if the phase isn't 'playing' — the guard mentioned back in lesson 6.

Invulnerability gets a visual cue too: a two-line addition at the top of drawShip() blinks the ship by skipping every other 100ms window while isInvulnerable() is true.

JavaScript
function drawShip() {
  if (isInvulnerable() && Math.floor(performance.now() / 100) % 2 === 0) return;
  // ...rest of drawShip unchanged
}

Restarting cleanly

resetGame() is deliberately exhaustive — it's the one place responsible for putting every piece of mutable state (ship, rocks, bullets, lives, score, timers) back to its starting value, then reseeding the field, so a restart is never subtly different from a fresh page load.

JavaScript
function resetGame() {
  state.phase = 'playing';
  state.ship.x = 0; state.ship.y = 0;
  state.ship.vx = 0; state.ship.vy = 0;
  state.ship.heading = -Math.PI / 2;
  state.ship.thrusting = false;
  state.ship.invulnerableUntil = performance.now() + RESPAWN_INVULN_MS;
  state.rocks = [];
  state.bullets = [];
  state.lives = 3;
  state.score = 0;
  state.spawn.timer = 0;
  state.difficulty.elapsed = 0;
  state.nextRockId = 1;
  state.timing.lastFrameTime = 0;
  seedRocks();
  overlayEl.classList.remove('visible');
  renderHud();
}

Two buttons call it: the always-visible Restart below the canvas, and the one inside the game-over overlay — same function, wired to both, so there's exactly one place that defines what "restart" actually means.
demoNote: Fly into a rock. You'll blink and get a couple invulnerable seconds instead of dying outright. Lose all three lives to see the game-over overlay, then hit Restart.
